title: Noetherian valuative properness test using discrete valuation rings
statement: Let $S$ be a locally Noetherian scheme [pqf-def-locnoeth], and let $f:X\to S$ be a finite-type morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Then $f$ is proper [def-weil-proper-morphism] if and only if for every discrete valuation ring $R$ [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], with fraction field $K$, and every pair of morphisms $a:\operatorname{Spec}K\to X$ and $b:\operatorname{Spec}R\to S$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] satisfying $f a=b|_{\operatorname{Spec}K}$, there exists a unique morphism $\widetilde a:\operatorname{Spec}R\to X$ such that $f\widetilde a=b$ and $\widetilde a|_{\operatorname{Spec}K}=a$. The DVR is not assumed of finite type over $S$ or excellent, and the generic point of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ need not map to a generic point of $S$.

proof.text: If $f$ is proper, it is separated by definition. A DVR is a valuation ring, as included in the equivalent characterization in [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. Apply [lemma-nagata-proper-separated-valuation-extension] to any of the stated DVR squares to obtain exactly the required unique lift. This proves the forward implication without a Noetherian hypothesis.

Assume the unique-DVR-lifting condition. Choose an affine open cover $S=\bigcup_i S_i$ with Noetherian coordinate rings, as in [pqf-def-locnoeth], and put $X_i=X\times_S S_i$. Finite type survives this base change by [lem-sfb-finite-type-composition-base-change]. The lifting condition survives too: compose a square over $S_i$ with $S_i\to S$; its lift to $X$, together with the prescribed map to $S_i$, gives a lift to $X_i$ by the fibre-product universal property. Two such lifts have the same projection to $X$ by the original uniqueness assumption and the same projection to $S_i$, hence coincide. By [lemma-nagata-projective-target-local] it suffices to prove properness of each $X_i\to S_i$. Relabel one such pair as $X\to S$. Now $S$ is affine Noetherian and $X$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian]; in particular $X$ is quasi-compact.

source.place: Tag 0208, first paragraph of (4) implies (1): reduction to an affine Noetherian base; the same argument applies to condition (3).

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-noetherian-dvr-closed-diagonal] to the Noetherian base and finite-type $f$. The assumed unique lifts imply its equality condition: two maps with the same base and generic restriction are lifts of the same square. Thus the diagonal is a closed immersion and $f$ is separated [def-weil-proper-morphism].

Apply [lem-weil-pbc-chow-noetherian] to the separated finite-type map $f$ over our Noetherian $S$. Obtain $\pi:X'\to X$ proper and surjective, and an immersion $i:X'\to P=\mathbf P^n_S$ with $qi=f\pi$, where $q:P\to S$ is proper by [lemma-nagata-projective-space-base-change-proper]. Proper morphisms are of finite type [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Hence $X'\to S$ is of finite type by composition [lem-sfb-finite-type-composition-base-change]; so both $X'$ and $P$ are Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian]. We only need properness and surjectivity of $\pi$; the birational refinement of Chow is unnecessary for condition (3), which tests every DVR square.

source.place: Tag 0208, second paragraph of (4) implies (1), Chow construction; Tag 0200 (coherent-lemma-chow-Noetherian).

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-dvr-proper-domination-closed-immersion] with $Y=X'$, the Chow maps $\pi,i$, and the projective structural map $q$. Here $X'$ is quasi-compact, $P$ is Noetherian, $\pi$ is proper, and $q$ is separated by its properness [def-weil-proper-morphism]. The existence part of the hypothesis on $f$ supplies exactly the required DVR lifts. Hence $i$ is a closed immersion.

Since $q$ is proper and $i$ is a closed immersion, [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-proper](b) makes $qi=f\pi$ proper, hence universally closed [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Surjectivity of $\pi$ and [lem-weil-pbc-image-universally-closed] give that $f$ is universally closed, and its final assertion gives properness since $f$ is separated and locally of finite type. Step 2 returns to the original base.
